outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace

args.reason: Inspect src/timing.js and briefly compare debounce with throttling.

outcomes.prose:
`debounce(fn, wait)` delays calling `fn` until no calls have occurred for `wait` milliseconds. Each new call cancels the previous timer, so only the latest arguments are used.

Use it when you care about the **final result after activity stops**, such as:

- Search requests while typing
- Validating form input
- Saving after the user pauses
- Handling window resize completion

Use **throttling** when you need execution at a controlled, regular rate during continuous activity, such as scrolling, dragging, or pointer movement.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace
outcomes.prose:
`debounce(fn, wait)` in `src/timing.js` returns a wrapped version of `fn`. Each call to the wrapper cancels any pending timer and starts a new `wait` ms timer. `fn` runs only after the wrapper has gone `wait` ms without being called. It runs once, with the arguments from the last call.

Limitations of this version:
- It has no leading-edge option, so it never fires at the start of a burst.
- It has no `cancel` or `flush` method.
- It drops the `this` binding, because the wrapper is an arrow function.
- It discards `fn`'s return value.

**Debounce vs. throttle**
- **Debounce** waits for activity to stop, then fires once. Use it when only the final value matters:
  - search-as-you-type requests
  - autosaving after edits
  - validating a field after the user stops typing
  - recomputing layout after a resize ends
- **Throttle** fires at most once per interval while activity continues. Use it when you need regular updates during a continuous stream:
  - scroll or drag handlers
  - mousemove tracking
  - progress reporting
  - game input

Debounce can starve. If events never pause for `wait` ms, `fn` never runs. If you need periodic updates during constant activity, use throttle.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] A one-line question gets a one-line answer
outcomes.prose: HTTP 418 means "I'm a teapot". It comes from RFC 2324, the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol, an April Fools' joke from 1998. A teapot that is asked to brew coffee responds with 418 because it refuses to do so. Some servers still use it as a playful or deliberate "I refuse" response, for example to turn away bots.
